- 1. For this question, please refer to our reply following the second and third official comments of reviewer u7bH.

- 2. As the reviewer mentioned, there are indeed some works that focus on preventing ambiguity attacks. They can be summarized into two categories: (1) Using multiple watermarking methods for joint verification [1] to increase the credibility of the verification, and(2) Employing a verification protocol to ensure secure verification [1,2,3]. 
    
      For the first category, our method can also be combined with other watermarking or fingerprinting techniques, and then voting can be performed to increase the reliability of the verification. For the second category, it is important to note that the methods for model verification and the protocols for model verification are two distinct concepts. The verification protocols involve the application of cryptographic techniques, such as symmetric encryption, to the embedded watermark information, with the aim of achieving secure watermark encryption, rather than focusing on more advanced watermark embedding methods. Currently, whether it is model fingerprinting or watermarking, the focus is mainly on the robustness of the method, i.e., whether the model can still be verified even after encountering removal attacks.

      Reference [3] also points out "reinforcing the link between the watermark and the model owner" as a measure, with the purpose of designing more robust verification methods, which is aligned with our goal. Therefore, designing robust verification methods to withstand various removal attacks is a more fundamental and basic solution.

- 3. When selecting benchmarks, we prioritize representative, easily reproducible, and widely recognized works. Regarding the work in [4], its performance does not seem to significantly outperform IPGuard and CAE (c.f. the experiment results reported in Tab. 2 and Tab. 6 from [4]). This suggests [4]'s experimental results do not demonstrate adequately superior robustness. Therefore, choosing the more superior performing UAP [5], which performs much better than IPGuard, as the latest benchmark appears to be a reasonable decision.

      Additionally, the works in [4] and [6] are both limited to the label-only black-box scenario, as they rely on prediction vector-based model outputs. Even though [4] proposes a "smooth-label probability" mitigation, it still experiences significant performance degradation when facing  Trans-A and Trans-L attacks (c.f. the experiment results reported in Tab. 4 from [4]).

      Another serious weakness of the approaches in [4] and [6] is the requirement to train multiple surrogate models beyond the source model. For example, [4] states "The defender first uses the source model as the teacher to train several surrogate models by knowledge distillation," and [6] needs to train thousands of models to construct model families. This raises practical concerns: in real-world scenarios, training a single model already requires substantial computation and data resources, so can the model owner realistically train a large model ensemble to implement the methods in [4] and [6]? This may also explain why existing fingerprinting works rarely adopt these two approaches as benchmarks.

T1%F is actually a representative point on the ROC curve. The plotting of the ROC curve can be referenced from the URL [1]. In the process of drawing the ROC curve, we initially classify all samples as one class, at which point both the TPR and FPR are 100%. Then, we gradually classify the samples into the other class one by one, calculating the TPR and FPR at each step. As all samples are gradually classified into the other class, the TPR and FPR will eventually be 0%. In this way, we complete the drawing of the ROC curve. ( The calculation code for the ROC curve in scikit-learn [2] follows the same approach). Additionally, although a set of thresholds can be pre-specified to assist in drawing the ROC curve, this pre-specification method is usually a suboptimal estimation of the ROC and cannot reach specific FPR values. For a specific FPR value, such as @0.1%FPR or @1%FPR, by gradually transitioning the classification of samples, it is possible to achieve an accurate specific FPR value. After computing and drawing the ROC curve, we select the corresponding TPR when the FPR is 1%, i.e., comparing the TPR under the same FPR condition. For example, in Figure 4a, we find the point on the y-axis that corresponds to the x-coordinate of 1%, which gives us the T1%F value. This allows us to avoid unfairly comparing the TPR at different FPR values by manually selecting the threshold. 

Additionally, we should notice that in the majority of works, the metric T1%F is usually directly used without a specific or formal definition. For instance, in [3], the authors state that "True Positive Rate when the False Positive Rate is at 1%, denoted as TPR@1%FPR". In [4] and [5], the metric TPR@0.1%FPR is used without any prior introduction or definition. Furthermore, in [6], the authors fix the FPR at $10^{-6}$ and compare the corresponding TPR, which can be expressed as T@0.0001%F in our case. Therefore, in our work, we do not formally define the T1%F or the detailed calculation process for this metric. Instead, we simply define it as "T1%F denotes True Positive Rate when the False Positive Rate is at 1%".

- 1 & 2: It is worth noting that the complete verification process involves two thresholds. The first threshold $Thr_\textit{mut}=0.5$ determines whether a given trajectory matches the source model (by comparing it to $r_\textit{mut}$). Specifically, for each trajectory, we compute the proportion of samples in the trajectory for which the model's predicted labels match the expected labels. The second threshold determines whether the suspect model is infringing (by comparing it to the detection rate). During this process, we calculate the proportion of trajectories that can be matched to the source model. As mentioned in Lines 229 of the paper:
  > The defender can determine whether $T_\textit{surf}$ is also the exclusive trajectory of $f_\textit{sus}$ by comparing the obtained $r_\textit{mut}$ and a threshold $Thr_\textit{mut}$ (0.5 in our case, equivalent to random guess). In practice, we calculate the detection rate of a number of adversarial trajectories (i.e. surface trajectories) on the suspect model to make the final infringement judgment. 

  For ADV-TRA, the Fingerprint Detection Rate is computed based on the surface trajectories $T_\textit{surf}$. This information can be found in Lines 231:
  > In practice, we calculate the detection rate of a number of adversarial trajectories (i.e. surface trajectories) on the suspect model to make the final infringement judgment.

  In other words, the Fingerprint Detection Rate is computed based on the respective unit of testing. In the baselines (which use samples to fingerprint), the unit of testing is the sample. However, in ADV-TRA, the unit of testing is the trajectory. In the definition provided in Lines 259, we do not clearly specify that the "fingerprinting samples" refer to the case in the baselines, and we apologize for the confusion this may have caused.


- 3. The T1%F metric is not the false positive rate of the model verification results. As defined in the caption of Table 2:
  > T1%F denotes True Positive Rate when the False Positive Rate is at 1%.

  Different fingerprinting methods for infringement determination use various thresholds, which in turn affect the false positive rates of the suspected models. For example, if we set the threshold to 1.0, the false positive rate for any method would be zero. To ensure a fair comparison that is not influenced by the choice of threshold, we avoid using threshold-dependent metrics. Instead, we use non-threshold-based metrics such as T1%F, T10%F, and AUC. These metrics reflect the ability of the fingerprinting samples or trajectories to distinguish the suspect models without being affected by different thresholds. They are standard metrics in the deep learning domain and have been used in many works [1-4]. Due to space constraints, we did not provide a formal definition of them in the paper.

- 4. In the algorithm, we formalize the number of queries for a surface trajectory $T_\textit{surf}$ as $2ml$. This value may vary depending on the dataset and application scenario. In the Implementation Details section of the Appendix (Lines 586), we have set the default values as $m = 10, l = 2$. Note that $l$ in this paper refers to the length of the initial trajectory $T_\textit{int}$, not the length of the surface trajectory $T_\textit{surf}$ which is created by concatenating $2m$ $T_\textit{int}$ (see Lines 175). Therefore, the verification of a single trajectory requires $2ml=40$ queries. In Appendix D.3.1, we control the length of $T_\textit{surf}$ by varying $l$ from 0 to 16, where the length referred to is also $2ml$. We use the term trajectory length here to provide a more intuitive representation of the number of queries, and to demonstrate that the verification overhead can be appropriately reduced by shortening the trajectory length, thereby achieving a better trade-off between the verification overheads and the performance.


We apologize for the lack of clarity in our paper regarding the selection of the second threshold used in our algorithm, as well as the definitions of the metrics employed in the experiments. We regret any misunderstanding this may have caused the reviewers. We will provide clearer and more comprehensive explanations for such metrics in the main text in the next version.

I am answering the first point.

**Definition of fingerprinting**

I do confirm that I have some expertise in fingerprinting. I understand this term as the usual and common definition that many communities agree on:
- biometrics (not to be confused with the "*biological domain*", as the authors wrote) 
- multimedia where fingerprint is also called a perceptual hash,
- computer forensics (browser fingerprinting, malware fingerprinting)
- PUF (Phyisically Unclonable Function) where fingerprint is also called an extracted feature from an object or device.

I did some work on all these applications of fingerprinting.

I recommend reading the following Wikipedia pages:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_fingerprint
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fingerprint_(computing)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Device_fingerprint

Quoting the last page: "A device fingerprint or machine fingerprint is information collected about the software and hardware of a remote computing device for the purpose of **identification**."

Moreover, I also did some works in IPP of DNN models. 


**IPP is not fingerprinting**

The authors partially agree with that statement since they wrote
> However, in IPP, the concept of fingerprinting has merely been adopted

This is indeed the crux of the problem: while acknowledging that IPP is different from fingerprinting, the authors continue to use the word fingerprinting. I clearly do not follow their rationale, which ought to cause confusion.

And confusion quickly happens: speaking about IPP
> "its specific meaning is to determine the identity of a model.*"

This is wrong: these schemes verify the identity of a model. They first make an assumption about the model in the black box: "Does the black box contain model X?" and the output is a Yes/No decision.

This is different from identification, where no assumption is made and the output is a model name. The distinction between verification and identification is well documented in fingerprinting literature. Note that fingerprinting can do both, while IPP can only do verification since the black box is queried with inputs dedicated to verify a given model X. 

**It is not the author's fault**

The authors argue that some authors already misuse the term fingerprinting in IPP literature and they got published. From now on, this legitimizes the use of the word fingerprinting in this domain.

What can I say here... Words have a meaning. The meaning of fingerprint in computer science has been settled for decades, and then, all of a sudden, this definition would be pulled down because someone got a paper published somewhere. I disagree; I prefer educating people rather than deliberately sustaining confusion. 

**References**
> A substantial body of surveys [1-3] and works [4-7]

I suppose that these references are the ones cited in the rebuttal of my comments (i.e. they do not come from the submitted paper, nor the rebuttal addressing comments of Reviewers y2LA or Reviewer TeCi).

[1] Deep Neural Network Fingerprinting by Conferrable Adversarial Examples. ICLR. 2021.

Clearly misuses the word fingerprinting.

[2] Copy, right? a testing framework for copyright protection of deep learning models. S&P. 2022.

Have you read this paper? The proposed technique, DeepJudge, is called "Testing". It is never presented as being fingerprinting.

[3] Intellectual property protection for deep learning models: Taxonomy, methods, attacks, and evaluations. IEEE TAI. 2021.

Clearly misuses the word fingerprinting.

[4] A systematic review on model watermarking for neural networks. Frontiers in big Data. 2021.

Have you read this paper? This survey is about watermarking, not fingerprinting.

[5] Revisiting the Information Capacity of Neural Network Watermarks: Upper Bound Estimation and Beyond. AAAI. 2024.

Have you read this paper? The word fingerprint never appears in this paper.

[6] Identifying appropriate intellectual property protection mechanisms for machine learning models: A systematization of watermarking, fingerprinting, model access, and attacks. IEEE TNNLS. 2023.

Have you really read this paper? This paper has nothing to do with our discussion on **passive** fingeprinting.
This paper is about **active** fingerprinting also known as traitor tracing "*We consider fingerprinting as an extension of watermarking.
While watermarking has the purpose to verify the owner of a digital asset, fingerprinting wants to trace its (potentially malicious) recipient.*"

[7] IPGuard: Protecting intellectual property of deep neural networks via fingerprinting the classification boundary. ACM CCS. 2021.

Clearly misuses the word fingerprinting.

**Conclusion**

There are papers entertaining this confusion [1, 3, 7]. There are papers not entertaining this confusion like [2] (speaks about testing, not fingerprinting) or "*FBI: Fingerprinting with Benign Inputs*" (truly uses a real fingerprint (since the inputs are not dedicated to a given model X) in the application of IPP).

Dear PC,

We have some reservations about the claims made by Reviewer u7bH with a confidence level of 5. There are two apparent misunderstandings or errors in his/her review:

- First, Reviewer u7bH has confused the meaning of fingerprinting in the biological domain and the deep learning domain. In Weakness 2, they stated that in deep learning IP protection, fingerprinting should be "identification via similarity search, not only verification." However, in IPP, the concept of fingerprinting has merely been adopted, and its specific meaning is to determine the identity of a model by observing its output on specific samples. A substantial body of surveys [1-3] and works [4-7] have provided clear definitions and categorizations of model fingerprinting. It is evident that Reviewer u7bH is not familiar with the specialized terminology, classifications, and principles of deep model IP protection, leading to a misevaluation of our work.

- Second, the reviewer does not seem to read our paper thoroughly. The reviewer misinterprets the Fingerprint Detection Rate metric in Table 1 as the False Positive Rate for model verification (the review states "This rate is only empirically measured, and it is rather high (between 1 and 10%)."). In fact, the final model infringement judgment is based on both the Fingerprint Detection Rate and a specified threshold. We have explained this point in multiple places throughout the paper (see Lines 259 and 265, and Section 2.2). What's more, the strength he/she pointed out are clearly erroneous. The reviewer commented: "The number of queries is relatively small." However, in the Design of ADV-TRA (see Figure 3), Limitations (see Appendix E), Impact of Trajectory Length (see Appendix D.3.1), and Implementation Details (see Appendix C), we have emphasized that "using trajectory fingerprints requires more query samples to obtain more accurate model decision boundary information." Hence it would be a weakness rather than a strength.

Thanks for your careful reading and useful feedback. Below, we will address your specific questions.

- Q1: This is an interesting question. ADV-TRA's mechanism offers valuable insights for other domains or neural network architectures. For example, in NLP, generating a batch of continuous text is difficult due to its discrete nature. However, on the embedding layer of NLP models, we can identify minimal perturbations on the continuous embeddings that affect predictions. Thus we can create trajectories in the embedding space, which can then be transformed into text as fingerprint trajectories.

- Q2: Compared to model watermarking, ADV-TRA has several significant advantages: (1) non-invasive: it does not require intervention in the model training process; (2) harmless: it does not degrade the model's performance; (3) unlimited capacity: there is no need to worry about the watermark capacity. Thus, ADV-TRA is more convenient and operable when deployed. Regarding robustness, since the robustness of model watermarking is highly correlated with the number of embedded watermark samples [1,2], and model fingerprinting does not have a capacity limit for verification samples, it is difficult to make a fair comparison between the two. Existing works [3,4] also analyze and compare the pros and cons of the two, and emphasize the feasibility of model fingerprinting during deployment. As for detectability, ADV-TRA only verifies the query results of adversarial trajectories, which is similar to the black-box model watermarking methods using adversarial samples [5,6]. The main downside of ADV-TRA is that it may require more query times to ensure precise probing of the decision boundary.

- Q3: We agree with the reviewer's perspective that the close-loop trajectory is better than the shorter one. In fact, we have carefully compared trajectories of different lengths (in terms of the number of class boundaries crossed) in Appendix D.2. Figure 9 shows that the trajectories crossing more classes achieve better performance. Moreover, the trajectories only crossing two classes (m=2) clearly cannot provide satisfactory verification performance. This suggests that longer trajectories can capture more "global" decision boundary information, thereby enabling more "unique" fingerprint extraction.

Thanks for your careful reading and useful feedback. We address your concerned points below.
- Q1&Q2&W3: We thank the reviewer for pointing this issue out. Regarding the main performance results in Table 1, we follow the evaluation methodology from previous works [1,2]. Specifically, We ran the experiments 5 times and calculated the standard deviation across 100 trajectories for each experiment. The standard deviation is calculated using the formula $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \overline{x})^2}{N-1}}$, where $\overline{x}$ is the mean value and $N=500$ for each type of suspect model. For each experiment, we build a new source model per dataset. We will include this information in the next version of the paper.
- Q3: It is a direct and straightforward approach of selecting a sample point as the starting point and forming a trajectory passing through multiple classes. However, non-contiguous trajectories (starting from multiple points) could lack connection between sub-trajectories, leading to information loss. Besides, using multiple starting points would require $m$ times more clean samples. Appendix D.2 also shows that longer trajectories crossing multiple classes can capture more unique fingerprints. 
- W1: Compared to other baselines, ADV-TRA has the lowest false positive rate (see Lines 264: "Only ADV-TRA ... guarantee the subsequent verification without any false positives"). We believe you may misunderstand the meaning of the Fingerprint Detection Rate metric (see Lines 259). It represents the proportion of fingerprinting samples (trajectories in our case) that are identified in a suspect model. Based on this metric, a threshold needs to be determined to classify the models as positive or negative (See Section 2.2). Considering that the thresholds vary for different methods, we do not perform a final judgment of ownership infringement, but instead directly show the discriminative ability of the fingerprinting samples on different models through the Fingerprint Detection Rate. Therefore, the Fingerprint Detection Rates for the negative models in Table 1 do not represent the False Positive Rate of the model verification.

  As for the second point, model watermarking also faces the challenge of forgery of ownership (also called ambiguity or overwriting attack) [3,4], where attackers can steal the source model and embed their own watermark to claim ownership. This is a recognized challenge in model IP protection, and not unique to model fingerprinting. In the field of model fingerprinting, we are more focused on the robustness of the fingerprints. Furthermore, in the second paragraph of the introduction, we compare model watermarking with fingerprinting. The embedding of watermarks can have a substantial impact on the source model, as described in work [3]: "During the watermark embedding, the training process of the classifier is modified, which may sacrifice the accuracy of the model." This is also why watermarking research tends to focus more on watermark capacity [5], as embedding too many watermarks can significantly degrade the model's utility.
- W2: We believe the reviewer confuses the definition of fingerprint in the biological and model IP protection (IPP) domains. In biological, fingerprints are unique biometric identifiers that can be used for identification. However, in the model IPP domain, the concept of a fingerprint is used differently. Model fingerprinting involves comparing sample-label pairs to verify a given model, rather than identifying a specific entity. The "suspect and verify" process mentioned by the reviewer is a special case where only one suspect model is involved. However, our algorithm can verify multiple suspect models simultaneously, similar to how criminal fingerprint comparison is used to identify suspects. Additionally, in the IPP domain, the concept of model fingerprinting is first defined by Cao et al. [7], and subsequent works [1,8,9] adopt this terminology. Relevant surveys [3,4,10] also provide clear definitions and categorizations of model fingerprinting.
- W4: Under the black-box verification mechanism, current model fingerprinting methods primarily rely on generating adversarial samples to probe the decision boundary and determine the ownership. This approach is effective for real-world scenarios. There are some other white-box methods [11,12] that observe the model's internal parameters or intermediate layer outputs. However, these white-box methods are not applicable in real-world settings. Therefore, in the black-box setting, using adversarial samples for verification is a primary means and serves as the baseline.

Thanks for your careful reading and useful feedback, and we address your specific questions below. 

- Q1 & W3: Thank you for pointing out this issue. We have discussed the issue of time overheads in Appendix D.5, which reflects the actual computational costs during the execution process. In fact, the model owner can perform model fingerprinting after the model training is complete, and store the fingerprinting samples locally to be used for future verifications. This means that the defense does not need to generate the fingerprinting samples every time a model verification is conducted. Therefore, we are not too concerned about the time overhead required for generating the fingerprinting samples in this domain.

- Q2: Thank you for pointing out this issue. In our experiments, we used a dataset of 10,000 samples that is separate from the training data of the source model for the fine-tuning process (as described in Appendix C). Therefore, the fine-tuning dataset and the source model's training dataset are different. However, as you mentioned, there could still be scenarios where an attacker fine-tunes the model using a significantly different dataset, such as fine-tuning a cat/dog classification model to become a face recognition model. In such cases, the training task and labels would have fundamentally changed, which is essentially watermarking or fingerprinting the pre-trained encoder [1,2], rather than the image classification model that we focus on in the paper. In real-world scenarios, attackers are more likely to simply steal the source model for the same task, as that would not require the additional effort of collecting and training on a different dataset for a new task, which would be computationally expensive. On the other hand, if the fine-tuning dataset is vastly different from the original training data, it would lead to a significant drop in the model's performance on the original task. This means the contribution of the source model would be diminished, and the attacker's own dataset and training efforts would play a larger role, potentially leading to disputes over the final model's ownership.

  To evaluate the impact of the fine-tuning dataset, we randomly selected 10 superclasses from the CIFAR-100 dataset and performed cross-training with CIFAR-10. Note that the labels in CIFAR-100 and CIFAR-10 do not overlap. The results are shown in the table below, where we also recorded the accuracy of the original task before and after fine-tuning. 
  |Original|CIFAR-10|CIFAR-10|CIFAR-100|CIFAR-100|
  |-|-|-|-|-|
  |__Fine-Tuning__|__CIFAR-10__|__CIFAR-100__|__CIFAR-10__|__CIFAR-100__|
  |__Original Acc__|0.870|0.870|0.712|0.712|
  |__Acc After Fine-Tuning__|0.863|0.117|0.133|0.701|
  |__IPGuard__|0.623|0.158|0.172|0.601|
  |__CAE__|0.676|0.134|0.116|0.659|
  |__UAP__|0.717|0.174|0.192|0.705|
  |__Ours__|0.760|0.195|0.208|0.747|
  We can find that our method achieves the highest fingerprint detection rate across all four cases, outperforming the negative model (see Table 1 in the main text). Additionally, the models fine-tuned using a different dataset experienced a significant drop in accuracy on the initial task. In other words, the fine-tuned models have largely lost their predictive capability on the original task. This also leads to a new consideration: a well-resourced attacker could simply train a model from scratch, rather than fine-tuning the source model on a different task, which could avoid potential intellectual property violations.

- W1 & W2: This is an interesting question. Even when SAST models are trained using the same dataset and training settings, they can still be successfully identified as negative models. The uniqueness of the model's decision boundary may be attributed to the randomness in model training (see Figure 8 in the Appendix). Similar experimental results have also been corroborated in works [3,4]. Furthermore, during the verification process, we selected 100 trajectories to capture more comprehensive decision boundary information, which helps avoid false positives due to high similarity in partial decision boundaries. It is recognized that two unrelated models will not exhibit similarity across all decision boundaries, thus preventing such "coincidental" false positives. Specifically, for malicious model thefts perpetrator, if they want to maintain the accuracy of the stolen model, they cannot drastically alter the model's decision boundary, which provides an opportunity for our detection method. Conversely, if the perpetrator significantly changes the decision boundary to evade detection, it would lead to a substantial decline in the model's usability, as supported by the findings in works [5,6,7].

summary.value:
The paper proposes a method to fingerprint deep neural networks in order to protect the model intellectual property. The authors focus on a technique post-training (without requiring changes to the training procedure), based on trajectories of adversarial examples called ADV-TRA. In contrast to other works that rely on adversarial examples that are highly sensitive to changes in the decision boundary, the technique aims to be more robust by constructing fixed-length trajectories with dynamic step sizes. The technique consists of four steps: (1) initialization of the trajectory; (2) probing the boundary; (3) bilaterize the trajectory; and (4) connect the trajectory. Among these, the second phase proposes a double optimization objective. First, to find adversarial examples at increasingly smaller steps, but proportional to two adjacent steps. Second, ensure that the adversarial examples are closer to the decision boundary than previously found adversarial examples.

The experiments consider several removal attacks (such as fine-tuning and pruning) and shows a lower false positive rate in detecting the fingerprint (negative suspect models are less often labeled as positive).

strengths.value:
1. The paper improves the false positives of the model fingerprinting and is more robust against the considered attacks. This was a limitation of prior work and the results compare with existing fingerprinting techniques. 


2. The authors creatively combine existing ideas about using adversarial examples and the decision boundary as a way to fingerprint the model. Based on the fact that model stealing attacks aim to increase fidelity, the authors propose to capture as much of the model’s decision surface to enable detection of model stealing attacks.

weaknesses.value:
1. The authors propose an application of model fingerprinting to tackle concerns in stealing the model parameters in both the black- and white-box setting. The strongest adversary in the context of model fingerprinting is an adaptive one that would try to steal the model while ensuring the decision boundaries are slightly different so targeting accuracy rather than accuracy *and* fidelity. 


2. How do we know that two unrelated models do not have the same fingerprinting? Ideally, we want model fingerprints to be akin to hashes, i.e., a small probability that two models that belong to two different owners would result in similar fingerprints. There is no theoretical reasoning or references for why this might be hard to achieve adversarially. In case there is a collision, how do we know which one is the “real owner”? Either of the model creators could have stolen the model or it could have happened that those trajectories are similar. 


3. While compared to watermarking techniques, this technique does not affect the training but there is still some optimization involved to construct these adversarial examples. There is no discussion about the computational costs.

questions.value:
1. What are the computational costs to run the defenses?

2. What happens if the fine-tuning dataset is not as similar as the training dataset. Could you give more details on that experiment? Basically, the hypothesis is that if the fine-tuning is not as similar, then the removal of the fingerprint is more likely.

summary.value: The paper proposes a novel fingerprinting scheme for DNN classifiers.

strengths.value: S1: The number of queries is relatively small (around 100)

weaknesses.value:
W1: The authors see fingerprinting only as a technical means for IP protection. Fingerprinting may have different applications. And, as IP protection is concerned, fingerprinting has strong limitations:
-  No theoretical guarantee, especially about the False Positive Rate. This rate is only empirically measured, and it is rather high (between 1 and 10%). I am sure that a judge would be convinced by this piece of evidence.
- The attacker can also exhibit a fingerprint which would prove that he is the owner of the stolen model. In other words, there is no secret key. Anyone can claim ownership of any model.
In short, I disagree with the 2nd paragraph comparing watermarking and fingerprinting.

W2. The name fingerprint is misleading. This is not a compact representation of a classifier. The defender must first suspect that THIS model is in the black box. Then he uses the trajectory of THIS model to query the black box, and based on the outputs, he computes a similarity with THIS model. Therefore, he can only make a verification for THIS model. This is in stark contrast to what people call a fingerprint in biometry or in multimedia security, ie a compact representation that allows identification via similarity search, not only verification. For instance, FBI [39] is a real fingerprinting scheme for DNN classifiers.

W3. The experimental setup is weak. If I understand correctly, the numbers are given for a unique source model (ie. ResNet 50 for ImageNet). Moreover, there are only 50 positive cases and 50 negative cases. I have difficulty understanding how the standard deviation of rates can be in the order of 10^-3 with so few examples. This accuracy would need millions of samples.

W4. The state-of-the-art (Sect. 2.2) and the benchmark are based on some former proposals, all based on adversarial examples. Other fingerprinting schemes not based on adversarial examples and boundaries are only listed in the appendices.

W5. The "fingerprint" extraction is not stealth. It is a series of very correlated inputs, easily detectable by the attacker at verification time.

questions.value:
Q1: Can you confirm that a unique source model is considered per dataset?

Q2: Can you explain how the standard deviation is computed?

Q3: Instead of connecting $m$ trajectories, which are not independent since they all depend on the starting point, would it be better to use $m$ independent trajectories starting from $m$ different points?

limitations.value: Some limitations are given (in the appendix, not the main body). Yet many others are missing: no theoretical guarantee, the attacker can play the role of a usurper, not stealth, and many queries to verify a "fingerprint".

summary.value: This paper introduces ADV-TRA, a fingerprinting scheme that uses adversarial trajectories to fingerprint DNN models. Unlike conventional methods that rely on single-point fingerprint samples, ADV-TRA generates a series of fixed-length trajectory samples, each showcasing varying levels of adversarial perturbation. Furthermore, the authors introduce an adaptive step-size adversarial trajectory generation algorithm capable of achieving fixed-length trajectories between any two classes through dynamically adjusted step sizes. ADV-TRA enhances the precision in capturing changes in the decision boundary, reducing the risk of misidentifying innocent models as infringing. Empirical experiments validate the uniqueness and robustness of ADV-TRA.

strengths.value:
- The paper proposes a black-box model ownership verification method using adversarial trajectories as fingerprints to measure the reuse relationship between two models.
- The effectiveness and robustness of this method are demonstrated through detailed and comprehensive experiments.

weaknesses.value:
- The related works on model fingerprinting discussed in this paper are mainly white-box methods or based on adversarial examples. However, testing-based fingerprinting methods such as [A, B, C] are not discussed in this paper.
- The proposed fingerprinting method may not apply to the models with different tasks and classes. Thus, it may not be robust to transfer learning.

[A] A Zest of LIME: Towards Architecture-Independent Model Distances. ICLR 2022.
[B] Are You Stealing My Model? Sample Correlation for Fingerprinting Deep Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2022.
[C] MetaV: A Meta-Verifier Approach to Task-Agnostic Model Fingerprinting. KDD 2022.

- Clarify whether the proposed method is robust to transfer learning.

summary.value: This work discusses a robust model fingerprinting method for protecting the intellectual property (IP) of deep neural networks (DNNs) using adversarial trajectories, referred to as ADV-TRA. Traditional single-point fingerprinting methods suffer from sensitivity to decision boundary changes, leading to high false positives. ADV-TRA overcomes this by generating a surface trajectory of adversarial examples that captures a comprehensive representation of the decision boundary, making it more resistant to various removal attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate ADV-TRA’s effectiveness in distinguishing between infringing and non-infringing models with low false positives, significantly outperforming previous methods. The proposed approach ensures a unique and reliable fingerprint with lower querying costs and proves robust against sophisticated adversarial attacks aimed at distorting or evading the model’s fingerprint.

strengths.value:
1. **Robustness Against Attacks**: ADV-TRA demonstrates superior resistance to removal attacks, including fine-tuning, pruning, and adversarial training. This robustness is crucial for practical deployment where models may face sophisticated threats aimed at circumventing IP protections.
2. **Low False Positive Rate**: The method achieves a low rate of false positives by using adversarial trajectories that provide a more granular and comprehensive analysis of the model's decision boundary. This reduces the likelihood of misidentifying legitimate models as infringing, a significant improvement over single-point fingerprinting techniques.
3. **Extensive Validation**: The paper conducts thorough experiments across multiple datasets against various removal attacks, providing strong empirical evidence of the method's effectiveness and practicality. This extensive testing helps in establishing the reliability of ADV-TRA in real-world scenarios.

weaknesses.value: **Complexity and Computational Costs**: The generation and verification of adversarial trajectories can be computationally intensive, potentially limiting the scalability of the method, especially for very large DNN models or in resource-constrained environments.

questions.value:
1. How well does ADV-TRA perform across various neural network architectures beyond those tested, such as transformer-based models or those used in non-visual tasks?
2. How does ADV-TRA compare to state-of-the-art model watermarking techniques regarding robustness, detectability, and ease of deployment?
3. Is the close-loop trajectory better than the shorter one?

title.value: United We Stand, Divided We Fall: Fingerprinting Deep Neural Networks via Adversarial Trajectories

abstract.value: In recent years, deep neural networks (DNNs) have witnessed extensive applications, and protecting their intellectual property (IP) is thus crucial. As a non-invasive way for model IP protection, model fingerprinting has become popular. However, existing single-point based fingerprinting methods are highly sensitive to the changes in the decision boundary, and may suffer from the misjudgment of the resemblance of sparse fingerprinting, yielding high false positives of innocent models. In this paper, we propose ADV-TRA, a more robust fingerprinting scheme that utilizes adversarial trajectories to verify the ownership of DNN models. Benefited from the intrinsic progressively adversarial level, the trajectory is capable of tolerating greater degree of alteration in decision boundaries. We further design novel schemes to generate a surface trajectory that involves a series of fixed-length trajectories with dynamically adjusted step sizes. Such a design enables a more unique and reliable fingerprinting with relatively low querying costs. Experiments on three datasets against four types of removal attacks show that ADV-TRA exhibits superior performance in distinguishing between infringing and innocent models, outperforming the state-of-the-art comparisons.

def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
